text: A 10-minute explanation of the complete predictive and prescriptive analytics workflow.
12 nodes  ·  24 canonical links  ·  1.59M source rows  ·  2022–2024 replay
The deck keeps the evidence, equations, limitations, and contribution split while removing repeated rubric slides.

Speaker 1, 25 seconds. Open with the project title and say that the group will cover the full workflow in three parts. Person 1 owns the foundation, Person 2 owns prediction and routing, and Person 3 owns DCRNN, research evidence, and the conclusion.
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
Countries are connected, so local stress can move through the network
Power flow changes every hour and can reverse direction
A busy interconnector can make neighboring paths important
The analyst needs both a forecast and an explainable action
Exact engineering ratings are incomplete in the supplied data
What should be investigated before the next operating window?
Predictive analytics estimates what may happen. Prescriptive analytics tests what could be done next.
Scope: recommendation-only screening. The prototype does not switch or dispatch a real grid.

Speaker 1, 55 seconds. Use the road analogy: countries are locations, interconnectors are roads, and power flow is traffic. The project asks what may happen next hour and which alternate route deserves engineering review. Emphasize that it is decision support, not automatic dispatch.

Parse UTC timestamps and align country histories
Check duplicates, missing cells, and timestamp gaps
Save processed artifacts before any model is trained
One target uses local, network, and static context
The model receives a tensor, not a raw CSV row.

Speaker 1, 60 seconds. Explain the two sources and the checks. Then explain the feature graph: local flow, load, imbalance, and load residual describe one country; global summaries describe the network; centrality describes static position. The model uses the previous 24 aligned hours and predicts the next hour.
Graph, risk screen, and loss assumptions

Dots are nodes; lines are canonical links; colors are screening states
Green = Normal   Amber = Warning   Red = Critical
Transparent proxy calculations with explicit limitations
Longer distance increases resistance when other assumptions stay fixed
Exact voltage, conductor area, and thermal ratings need engineering data

Speaker 1, 60 seconds. Explain that the graph gives topology and neighboring relationships. The risk screen combines flow pressure, imbalance, and load forecast error. The loss equations use distance-derived length and assumed constants, so the result is a proxy estimate, not a full AC power-flow calculation. Handoff to Person 2.
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
The website chooses from simple rules using chronological holdout error
Persistence: next hour equals the latest observed flow
Moving average: mean of the latest 24 hours
Seasonal naive: same hour on the previous day
Linear trend: fit a line to the recent window
Used in the saved experiment comparison

Python handles ingestion and APIs. NumPy supports arrays. PyTorch trains the neural models. Matplotlib and the saved JSON/CSV files support the evidence pack. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript render the dashboard.

Speaker 2, 55 seconds. Explain the simple models first. State clearly that the live website currently uses the selected Persistence baseline. Fusion GRU and DCRNN are trained research comparisons in the results pack. Mention the library roles only at the level needed for the audience.
How the next-hour prediction is made
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
If the selected model is Persistence
The same chronological holdout is used for fair comparison
A prediction is also classified as Normal, Warning, or Critical using historical thresholds. MAPE is reported for completeness but can be unstable near zero or when flow changes sign.

Speaker 2, 55 seconds. Use the numerical example. Explain that the website forecast can be simple because the latest hourly value is a strong short-horizon baseline. Then define the error metrics and stress classes. The model is selected by the lowest pooled RMSE on a chronological holdout.
Performance evidence from the saved run
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
Lower RMSE is better; higher F1 is better
Persistence RMSE 580.3 MW · Fusion GRU 570.5 MW · DCRNN 634.0 MW
Rows = actual class · columns = predicted class

Speaker 2, 60 seconds. Point out that Fusion GRU has the lowest RMSE among the saved trained models, while Persistence remains the operational selection in the website artifact. Explain that the confusion matrix reveals the type of stress-class mistakes. Do not call accuracy proof of safety.
Prescriptive routing: from stress to a reviewable option
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
Power is treated as flow moving across connected lines
Move 25% of the selected flow, then test whether the alternate path has space.
The planner explains accepted and rejected paths
Moved MW = current flow × reroute percentage
Reject links with insufficient headroom or Critical risk
Rank survivors by distance, utilization, and estimated loss
Show before/after loading, loss delta, bottlenecks, and confidence
Purple route means recommendation; engineer validates it
Route Found · Best Effort Review · No Route

Speaker 2, 60 seconds. Explain that routing is a what-if calculation. For 1,000 MW and a 25% reduction, the planner tests 250 MW on alternate paths. It rejects paths without enough proxy headroom or with Critical risk and ranks the survivors. It does not physically redirect electricity.
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
It reads time and neighboring nodes together
Road analogy: before predicting traffic on one road, DCRNN also checks nearby roads.
DCRNN is more complex and slower in this saved run
Local history already explains much of the short-horizon flow
The supplied topology and features are proxies, not full grid state
Keeping DCRNN in the comparison is still a valid research result

Speaker 3, 60 seconds. Explain DCRNN as a memory model that also passes information across neighboring countries. Then state the actual result: graph context did not win this run. The reasons are dataset size, proxy topology, missing physical state, and strong local autocorrelation. This is evidence about this experiment, not a claim that DCRNN is always weak.

Validation behavior matters more than training loss alone
Thresholds change the balance between misses and false alarms
Validation MAE increase after shuffling a feature
What the model handles well and where it breaks
Stable recent flow is easier. Abrupt movement and class-boundary changes are harder.

Speaker 3, 60 seconds. Point to the four evidence types: training/validation behavior, threshold curves, feature importance, and qualitative errors. The feature chart shows that recent local net flow is the strongest signal in this run. The error examples demonstrate why a model can be accurate overall and still fail during abrupt changes.

Future work: verified ratings, N-1 analysis, calibrated uncertainty, telemetry

Speaker 3, 55 seconds. Explain the integration contract from CSV to browser. Then state the novelty carefully: transparent integration, model selection by evidence, explicit proxy physics, and route guardrails. Close with the real limitations: no certified engineering ratings, no N-1 security study, no real telemetry adapter, and no automatic control.

Prediction answers: what may happen next?   Routing answers: what option should be investigated?   Validation answers: can we trust the result enough to review it?

Speaker 3, 45 seconds. Summarize the complete workflow in one sentence. State each person’s contribution using the three labels on the slide. End with the limitation that the prototype supports engineering review and does not authorize real-grid action. Invite questions.
